skill.name: Formal or informal: matching the reader
skill.why: The same message needs different words for a principal and for a mate.
skill.how: Check who's reading and why. Then pick words that fit them.

steps.say: Before I write, I ask: who's reading? Here's one question, said three ways.

show.text: Wanna come to the footy this arvo?
Can you come to the footy this afternoon?
show.nudge: That's fine, but a bit careful for a best mate. Which one sounds like chatting?

show.text: Would you like to attend the football this afternoon?
show.nudge: That sounds like a letter! Would you text your best mate that?

steps.ask: Tap the one you'd text your best mate.
steps.win: Yes! 'Wanna' and 'arvo' are informal, for mates. The last one is formal. The middle sits in between.

steps.say: It's a scale, from relaxed to careful. The less you know the reader, the more careful you get.

show.nudge: That's how you greet a mate. Wren hardly knows Dr Lin.
Friendly, but a bit chatty for a vet she's met once.
Too stiff! Wren knows her name, so she can use it.

steps.ask: Wren is writing to a vet she met once. Tap the best opening.
steps.win: Yes! Careful, but it still uses her name. Too chatty and too stiff are both wrong here.

steps.say: Careful! More formal is not always better. Tully is making a sign for five-year-olds.
steps.ask: Which line fits a sign for five-year-olds?

options.text: Participants must wear suitable headwear.
options.reason: Preps won't know those words. It's far too stiff for five-year-olds.

options.text: Hi, Preps! Bring a hat and a big smile!
Hats. Now. No excuses.
options.reason: That's bossy, not friendly. Little kids need warm, simple words.

steps.win: Yes! Warm and simple fits little kids. Too formal is just as wrong as too casual.

steps.say: Fancy words can still sound rude. Mo is writing to the mayor about the oval.
steps.ask: Which line fits a letter to the mayor?

options.text: We require the oval to be fixed immediately.
options.reason: It sounds formal, but 'require' and 'immediately' boss the mayor around.

options.text: Can you fix the oval? It's so bad lol.
options.reason: 'Lol' and 'so bad' are chat words for mates. The mayor needs careful ones.

options.text: We respectfully ask you to fix the oval.

steps.win: Yes! Formal and polite: it asks, it doesn't boss. That fits someone important you don't know.

steps.say: One chatty word can spoil a careful letter. Find it in Indi's email.
show: Dear Mr Bell, thank you for the

show.nudge: That's just the place. Which word sounds like chatting with a mate?
That's just the day. Which word is chatty?

steps.ask: Tap the word that's too casual for Mr Bell.
steps.win: Yes! 'Awesome' is chatty. 'Excellent' is warm but careful, so it fits.

terms.means: Relaxed words for mates and family, like 'Hey', 'wanna' and 'arvo'.
Careful, polite words for people you don't know well, or serious jobs.

examples: thank you for helping our wombat.
card.test: It's a scale. Who's reading? The less you know them, the more careful. Too stiff can be wrong too.

weDo.text: Mo is writing to the school principal, Ms Lee. He wants to ask if the crew can use the hall for a cooking show.
weDo.prompt: Which opening fits a letter to the principal?
weDo.hint: Who is reading? Pick the words you'd use with the principal.
weDo.success: 'Dear Ms Lee, I am writing to ask' is polite and careful, just right for a principal.

options.text: Yo Lee! Gimme the hall, yeah?
options.reason: That's how you'd talk to a mate. A principal needs polite words.

options.text: Dear Ms Lee, I am writing to ask if we could use the hall.
Hey Ms Lee! Can we have the hall?
options.reason: 'Hey' and the ! sound like a chat in the corridor. How do letters to a principal begin?

weDo.prompt: Mo is texting his best mate, Gus. Tap the line that's far too formal for a mate.
weDo.hint: Which line sounds like a letter from the bank, not a text to a mate?
weDo.success: 'I would be most grateful for your prompt reply' is for business letters. To a mate, say 'Let me know!'

parts.tap: Hey Gus!
parts.reason: That's a friendly, relaxed way to start a text to a mate.

parts.tap: Wanna come to the beach this arvo?
parts.reason: 'Wanna' and 'arvo' are relaxed words. They fit a text to a mate.

parts.tap: I would be most grateful for your prompt reply.
Bring snacks!
parts.reason: Short and cheeky. That's how mates text each other.

creature.name: Dappella
creature.blurb: A superb fairy-wren that puts on smart blue feathers for important readers and plain brown ones for its mates. It always checks who's listening first.

write.ask: Rewrite Zed's message for the principal. Keep what he is asking for.
given: Hey Ms Lee, can we have a gaming club in the library? It'd be epic.
checks: I used polite words, such as could and please
It still asks for a gaming club
write.model: Dear Ms Lee, could we please start a gaming club in the library at lunchtime?

encounters.frame: A Dappella is watching Tully write a letter at the hut table.
encounters.text: Tully is writing a letter to the mayor of Scaffold Peaks. She wants new goalposts for the snow oval. The old ones are bent and rusty. One fell over last week and nearly squashed a goat. The mayor is a busy, important person. Tully has never met her. She has drawn a picture of the goat to go with the letter. She wants the mayor to take her letter seriously.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence fits Tully's letter to the mayor?
encounters.success: Polite words like 'could' and 'please' fit an important reader like the mayor.

options.reason: This is how you'd talk to a mate. The mayor needs polite, careful words.

options.text: Could you please arrange new goalposts for the snow oval?
Can you get us some new goalposts?
options.reason: No please, and 'get us' sounds like asking a mate. How would you ask someone important?

Mo

encounters.frame: The Year 5 class is writing to the council about Pebble Bay. The Dappella flew down to help.
encounters.text: The Year 5 class is writing a letter to the Pebble Bay Council. Every weekend, the beach bins overflow, and rubbish blows into the sea. Last month, a seal pup got tangled in a chip packet and had to be rescued. The class wants the council to put out more bins before summer. The councillors meet next Tuesday to decide what to spend money on. They are busy adults, and none of them knows the class. Tully has been chosen to write the most important sentence of the letter, the one that asks for help. The class wants the councillors to take them seriously.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence should Tully use in the letter to the council?
encounters.success: 'We are asking the council' is clear and polite, so the councillors will take the class seriously.

options.text: Seriously, guys, the bins are a total joke, so just chuck in a few more.
options.reason: 'Seriously, guys' and 'a total joke' are how you'd moan to mates, not ask a council.

options.text: Hi everyone, could you please chuck a few more bins down at Pebble Bay?
options.reason: It's polite, but 'Hi everyone' and 'chuck' are chatty. Busy strangers need more careful words.

options.text: We are asking the council to put more bins at Pebble Bay before summer.

encounters.frame: Gus's latest experiment went badly. The Dappella has slime on its tail feathers.

encounters.frame: Indi is visiting the Prep class to talk about the moon. The Dappella is hiding in her bag.
encounters.text: Indi has been asked to give a talk about the moon to the Prep class at Scaffold Peaks Primary. The Preps are five years old. They will be sitting on the carpet in front of her, and some of them can't read yet. Their teacher, Ms Ford, has given Indi five minutes. 'Keep it simple and fun,' Ms Ford said. 'If they get bored, they start rolling around.' The Preps will have just come in from lunch, so they will be full of energy. Indi has made a big paper moon with craters drawn on in grey pencil, and she plans to let each child touch it at the end. She has also brought a torch, so she can show how the moon only shines because the sun lights it up. The hardest part, Indi thinks, will be the very first sentence. It has to grab the little ones straight away, before anyone starts rolling.
encounters.prompt: Which opening fits Indi's talk to the Prep class?
encounters.success: A friendly hello and a simple question suit five-year-olds. They can answer it and start listening.

options.text: Today I will explain why the moon appears to shine at night.
options.reason: 'I will explain' and 'appears' sound like a lesson for older kids. Preps need it simple and fun.

options.text: The moon is 384,400 kilometres away and covered in craters.
options.reason: A giant number means nothing to a five-year-old. Ms Ford asked Indi to keep it simple.

options.text: Hi, everyone! Have you ever looked up and seen the moon at night?
Good afternoon, everyone. My name is Indi, and my talk is about the moon.
options.reason: This is polite but stiff, like a speech to grown-ups. It won't grab Preps before they start rolling.

encounters.frame: A real cellist visited Scaffold Peaks Primary. The Dappella is helping Lila thank her.
encounters.text: Last week, a professional cellist named Ms Valentina Ruiz climbed all the way up to Scaffold Peaks Primary to play for the senior students. She carried her cello up four ladders on her back, wrapped in three blankets to keep out the cold. For an hour, she played music from all over the world and answered every question the students asked, even Gus's question about whether a cello could be played underwater. At the end, she let six students try her cello, which is two hundred years old. The principal has asked Lila to write a thank-you email to Ms Ruiz on behalf of the whole school. Ms Ruiz is an adult the students met only once. Lila has written most of the email, and it is warm and polite. She has also attached a photo of the whole school waving goodbye. Now she needs a final sentence, and the principal will read it before it is sent.
encounters.prompt: Which final sentence fits Lila's thank-you email to Ms Ruiz?
encounters.success: A warm, polite thank-you suits a professional guest. It shows the whole school valued her visit.

options.reason: 'Thanks heaps' and a joke for the cello are matey. Ms Ruiz is a professional the school met once.

options.reason: This sounds like a business receipt. Lila's email is meant to be warm as well as polite.

options.reason: Lila writes for the whole school, so her own favourite song doesn't belong in the last line.

options.text: Thank you again for giving up your time to visit our school.

encounters.frame: Year 6 is writing to the Minister for the Environment. The Dappella has never seen the class so serious.
encounters.text: For a whole term, Year 6 at Scaffold Peaks Primary has been studying Pebble Bay, the small cove at the foot of the island. They have counted the fish in its rock pools, photographed the seals that sunbake on its ledges and collected more than four thousand pieces of plastic from its sand. Their research shows that the bay is home to at least eleven kinds of fish found almost nowhere else, but that boats and rubbish are slowly damaging it. The class has decided to write to the Minister for the Environment, who has the power to turn the bay into a marine sanctuary. The Minister receives hundreds of letters every week and does not know anyone at the school. Ms Ford has warned the class that only letters that are respectful, serious and clearly written will be read past the first line. The class has also collected three hundred signatures from around the island. Wren has been chosen to write that first line, the one that asks for the sanctuary. The rest of the letter will include the fish count and a map of the bay. If it works, Pebble Bay could be protected for a hundred years.
encounters.prompt: Which first line should Wren use in the letter to the Minister?
encounters.success: 'We respectfully ask' is formal and polite. A Minister reads many letters and takes careful ones seriously.

options.text: Our whole class insists that you make Pebble Bay a marine sanctuary.
options.reason: 'Insists' bosses the Minister about. Ms Ford asked for a respectful letter.

options.text: We respectfully share our research on the rare fish of Pebble Bay.
options.reason: It's careful and polite, but this first line has to ask for the sanctuary.

options.text: We respectfully ask that you protect Pebble Bay as a marine sanctuary.
Hi Minister, we would be so grateful if you protected Pebble Bay.
options.reason: 'Hi' and 'so grateful' are chatty. A Minister who doesn't know you needs a careful tone.

encounters.frame: Wren's little cousin is coming to stay in the hut on Crag Tower. The Dappella helped draw the possums.

encounters.success: Warm, personal words help a scared seven-year-old feel safe. 'An adult will supervise' sounds like a notice.

options.text: It's warm and personal, so a scared Poppy feels safe with Wren.
It's more formal, so Poppy can tell that Wren will take care of her.
options.reason: It's less formal, not more. Formal words would sound like a notice to Poppy.

options.text: It sounds like a rule, so Poppy will remember to stay close.
options.reason: 'An adult will supervise' is the one that sounds like a rule. Wren's line is a promise.

options.reason: Neither line is rude, and the letter is written for Poppy, not her mum.

encounters.text:
Wren's cousin Poppy is seven. Next week she is coming to stay at the hut on Crag Tower, and she has heard all the ghost stories from the older kids at school. Last night Poppy sent Wren a wobbly drawing of a ghost with the words 'I'm scared' written underneath in purple crayon. Wren is writing back to cheer her up. Poppy has never stayed away from home before, and her mum says she has been sleeping with the light on. Wren wants Poppy to feel safe and excited, not worried.

Hi Poppy! Thank you for your drawing. Don't worry, the hut isn't haunted, it's just full of possums. The scratching noises at night are just the possums having a midnight snack. One of them is called Biscuit, and he loves apple. If you're brave, you can feed him a slice. The hut has a big fireplace and a window where you can see the stars. I'll be right there with you, and we'll make hot chocolate with marshmallows. Bring your pyjamas with the penguins on them. Mo is cooking pancakes, but don't worry, I'll make sure they're normal ones. See you soon!
Love, Wren

encounters.frame: Wren and Ranger Kim are writing up their quoll survey. The Dappella spotted a phrase that doesn't fit.
encounters.prompt: Tap the words that are too casual, then choose a better word.

parts:
Wren and Ranger Kim are writing up their quoll survey for the Alpine Wildlife Journal, which is read by scientists across the country. Every report in the journal is checked by experts before it is printed, and anything chatty is sent back to be rewritten.

Survey of spotted-tailed quolls, Snow Gum Gully
In June, we set twelve motion-sensing cameras along the creek in Snow Gum Gully. The weather was cold, with snow on eleven of the twenty-eight nights. Over four weeks, the cameras recorded sixty-three sightings of spotted-tailed quolls. Most sightings occurred between midnight and four in the morning. Ranger Kim identified each quoll by the pattern of white spots on its back. Two cameras were knocked over, probably by wombats, and had to be reset. On 19 June, we located a den beneath a fallen snow gum. The den contained a female and four young, all of which appeared

parts.tap: in good nick

parts: . The female was

parts.tap: observed
parts.reason: That's fine. 'Observed' is the careful word scientists use.

parts: carrying food to the den on three separate nights. No foxes were recorded within two hundred metres of the den. We

parts.tap: recommend
parts.reason: That's fine. 'Recommend' is formal and clear, right for a journal.

parts: that the gully be closed to campers until the young are old enough to leave the den. A full table of sightings is attached. This survey was funded by the Scaffold Peaks Council.

encounters.frame: Gus is presenting Sprocket to the Island Robot Challenge judges. The Dappella is holding his notes.
encounters.text: Gus has made it to the final of the Island Robot Challenge. On Saturday he must stand in front of the judging panel and explain how Sprocket works. Each finalist has exactly three minutes. The panel is made up of three engineers: one builds bridges, one designs ski lifts, and one has spent twenty years making robots for hospitals. The bridge engineer is famous for asking 'How?' after every sentence. They will score each finalist on how well the robot works and how clearly its builder can explain it. Last year, a finalist lost points for saying his robot was 'basically magic'. Gus has practised his speech in front of the crew four times, and Mo has fallen asleep three of them. Tully has calculated that he has a 41 per cent chance of winning. Gus has cut every joke from the speech except one, and his notes are covered in grease and one chocolate fingerprint. He has written most of it, but he is stuck on the sentence that explains how Sprocket actually clears snow. Indi has reminded him that the judges are experts, and they want facts, not hype. The winner gets a trophy and a week at a real robotics lab.
encounters.prompt: Which sentence should Gus use to explain Sprocket to the judges?
encounters.success: Exact, technical words suit a panel of engineers. They want to know how Sprocket works, clearly and calmly.

options.text: Sprocket's got two spinny brushes and a hot-air blower that gets the snow right off the ladders.
options.reason: 'Spinny' and 'gets the snow off' are chatty. Engineers want each part named exactly.

options.text: Sprocket uses two rotating brushes and a heated air nozzle to clear snow from ladder rungs.
Sprocket clears snow really well, which is exactly why it works so brilliantly.
options.reason: This says it works, but not how. The bridge engineer would ask 'How?' straight away.

options.text: Sprocket is the most advanced snow-clearing robot ever built on this island.
options.reason: This is hype, not facts. Indi warned Gus that the judges want to know how it works.

encounters.frame: The Snowcats are hosting Pine Gully on Saturday. The Dappella is reading Tully's email before she sends it.
encounters.prompt: Tap the sentence that is too casual for an email to Coach Daniels.
encounters.success: It has no slang, but reminding rivals of last season is a dig. The email must stay courteous.

parts:
Tully is the junior captain of the Snowcats. This Saturday, the Pine Gully Possums are travelling to Scaffold Peaks for a match, and the club has asked Tully to email their coach, Mr Daniels, to welcome the team and explain the arrangements. Tully has never met Coach Daniels. Her own coach has reminded her that the email represents the whole club, so it must be courteous and clear, even though the two teams are fierce rivals. Last season the Possums won by a single point, and some Snowcats fans have not forgiven them.

Dear Coach Daniels,

parts.tap: On behalf of the Snowcats, I would like to welcome your team to Scaffold Peaks for Saturday's match.
parts.reason: This is courteous and formal, a good way to welcome a visiting coach.

parts.tap: The game will begin at 10 am on the snow oval, and lunch will be provided afterwards in the clubrooms.
parts.reason: Clear arrangements in careful sentences are exactly what a coach needs.

parts: Your bus can park at the bottom station, and our players will help carry your bags up the ladders.

parts.tap: Our players have certainly not forgotten last season's one-point loss.
Please let me know if any of your players have food allergies.
parts.reason: A polite request about the players' needs fits a formal welcome email.

parts: If it snows heavily, the match will move to Sunday at the same time.

parts.tap: We look forward to a great game.
parts.reason: A friendly, polite ending suits an email to another club.
